source.title: Kernel Methods and Multi-layer Perceptrons Learn Linear Models in High Dimensions
source.authors: Mojtaba Sahraee-Ardakan; M. Emami; Parthe Pandit; Sundeep Rangan; Alyson K. Fletcher

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures test error across training epochs and training-sample counts, using experiments on kernel, linear, and neural-network models. It does not use the original double-descent recipe, and the supplied text does not state the curve shapes.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on double descent but those cited findings are not its own results. Its own experiments plot test error over epochs and sample counts; the supplied text reports model-equivalence comparisons but does not describe the fall-rise-fall shapes. The figures are not rendered in the supplied text, so plotted values and curve directions cannot be extracted.
record.test_reason: Double descent appears only as motivation in the abstract and in cited prior work. The paper's own results show that kernel and NTK models equal regularized linear models under proportional, uniform high-dimensional assumptions. Its experiments plot test error against sample count (Figs 1, 3) and against epochs (Fig 2). They use fixed ridge regularization (λ=0.005, or the optimal λ=σ²), sweep no model size, and the text never describes a peak, a fall-rise-fall shape, or error rising with more data. The results therefore do not bear on whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Under assumptions A1–A3, kernel methods and NTK-regime networks learn only linear models, which are even Bayes-optimal for GP data. The authors frame this as a limitation of those assumptions, not of nonlinear models.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes kernel-to-linear equivalence and compares test errors in high-dimensional settings; it does not reproduce the original double-descent experiments or sweep model capacity to locate an interpolation peak.
record.method_sensitivity: In Section 6.1, the finite-width neural network matches the NTK and linear-model errors for small sample counts and follows them closely otherwise.

fits_no_version.finding: Under proportional, uniform i.i.d.-covariate asymptotics, kernel ridge regression (including the NTK of wide fully connected nets) matches a suitably regularized linear model. The match holds at convergence and at every gradient-descent step, with near-identical test error across n and epochs. The equivalence breaks for low-rank mixture inputs (Fig 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the proportional uniform high-dimensional regime used in many double-descent analyses, kernel/NTK learners reduce to linear ridge models, so their risk curves are those of linear models.

record.problems: The supplied text does not include rendered figures or numerical curve values, so the plotted shapes cannot be assessed. The text reports averages over runs but no error bars, confidence intervals, or other uncertainty estimates.

untested.parts: all; epoch curves are reported only as NN–linear agreement, with no peak described
all; no interpolation threshold or rising error with n is reported
all; regularization is fixed, not varied against a peak

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' guess for V2 and V3 is unsupported: the curves serve only to show model equivalence, with fixed or optimal regularization. Rows r4 and r9 are reference curves (oracle and theoretical optimum), not results.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over model size or capacity is reported.
The text does not report whether test error follows a fall-rise-fall curve or where a peak occurs; the figure's plotted trajectory is unavailable.
The text does not establish that the sample counts include values near an interpolation threshold, nor does it state whether increasing sample count raises test error there.
No capacity sweep testing general double descent across model classes is reported.
No single effective-complexity measure is proposed or tested as predicting peak locations.
The experiments do not test whether noise or regularization drives or removes a double-descent peak, or whether multiple peaks occur.
The paper does not compare the curve against an effective parameter count to test whether a second descent becomes an ordinary U-shape.
